RZig

RZig lets R package authors write plain Zig functions and generate safe .Call bindings without C++ or hand-written SEXP conversion code.

Requirements

  • R and the platform toolchain used to build R source packages: Xcode command-line tools on macOS, Rtools on Windows, a C compiler and the R development headers on Linux.
  • Zig of the 0.16 or 0.17 release series (0.16.x or 0.17.x), needed only to install a package created with RZig. RZig itself, its examples and its tests run without Zig. Zig changes its language and standard library between release series, so other versions are rejected with a message naming the version found.

Code that has to build with both series is best formatted with the zig fmt of Zig 0.16: the formatter of Zig 0.17 rewrites @intFromEnum and @enumFromInt into the builtins @backingInt and @fromBackingInt, which Zig 0.16 does not have.

configure compiles the Zig code for the platform of R: x86_64 or arm64 macOS for the macOS version that R links for (MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET, or that of libR.dylib), x86_64 or arm64 Linux with glibc or musl, and x86_64 or arm64 Windows. RZIG_ZIG_TARGET names another Zig target, for example RZIG_ZIG_TARGET=x86_64-linux-musl.

Download Zig from https://ziglang.org/download/ and confirm the version:

zig version
# 0.16.0

Install RZig

From CRAN:

install.packages("rzig")

The development version from GitHub:

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("MarekDejaUJ/rzig")

If Zig is not on PATH, tell RZig where it is:

Sys.setenv(ZIG = "/absolute/path/to/zig")

find_zig() and the generated package configuration search in this order: ZIG, PATH, ~/.local/share/zig/*/zig, then ~/zig/zig. An R session launched from an IDE may not inherit variables exported by a shell; in that case, set ZIG with Sys.setenv() first.

rzig::find_zig(required = FALSE)
#> Zig compiler: /usr/local/bin/zig (version 0.16.0, supported)
#> rzig supports Zig 0.16.x or 0.17.x.

Create a working package

The workflow has five steps, each an R function. For a copy-paste-safe example, create the package in R’s session temporary directory. Replace tempdir() with an explicit project directory when keeping the result.

1. Scaffold. use_rzig() adds the build files, the framework sources and a starter src/rzig/src/main.zig with a working hello_zig() function:

pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "rzhello")
dir.create(pkg)
writeLines(
  c(
    "Package: rzhello",
    "Type: Package",
    "Title: A Small RZig Example",
    "Version: 0.0.1",
    "Authors@R: person('Your', 'Name', email = 'you@example.org', role = c('aut', 'cre'))",
    "Description: Demonstrates a Zig implementation called safely from R.",
    "License: GPL-3",
    "Encoding: UTF-8"
  ),
  file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION")
)
rzig::use_rzig(pkg)
#> Generated RZig bindings for rzhello: 1 exported function
#> Created RZig scaffold for package rzhello

2. Write Zig. Open src/rzig/src/main.zig, keep its imports, panic declaration and comptime registration block, and replace the generated hello_zig() function with:

/// Add two numeric vectors elementwise.
/// @param a The first numeric vector.
/// @param b The second numeric vector.
/// @return The elementwise sums.
/// @export
pub fn add_vectors(
    ctx: *rzig.Ctx,
    a: []const f64,
    b: []const f64,
) rzig.Error![]f64 {
    if (a.len != b.len) {
        return rzig.raise("lengths differ: {d} vs {d}", .{ a.len, b.len });
    }
    const result = try ctx.alloc(f64, a.len);
    for (a, b, result) |left, right, *value| value.* = left + right;
    return result;
}

The @param and @return lines are optional. When they are absent, document() generates neutral placeholders from the Zig signature. Only /// @export is required to expose a public function to R. Exported functions are top-level pub fn declarations starting at the beginning of a line, as zig fmt writes them.

3. Scan. scan_exports() lists what R will see, with the R value of every parameter and of the return value:

rzig::scan_exports(pkg)
#> Zig exports of package rzhello (src/rzig/src/main.zig): 1 function
#>
#> add_vectors(a, b)
#>   a          []const f64            double vector, borrowed
#>   b          []const f64            double vector, borrowed
#>   returns    rzig.Error![]f64       double vector

4. Generate. document() writes the Zig manifest, the R wrappers and the NAMESPACE block; render_bindings() shows the same texts without writing them, and rzig_status() reports whether every step is complete:

rzig::document(pkg)
#> Generated RZig bindings for rzhello: 1 exported function
rzig::rzig_status(pkg)
#> RZig status of package rzhello
#>   [ok] DESCRIPTION   package rzhello
#>   [ok] Scaffold      build files and framework sources present
#>   [ok] Zig source    src/rzig/src/main.zig
#>   [ok] Exports       1 function: add_vectors
#>   [ok] Bindings      generated files match the exports
#>   [ok] Zig compiler  /usr/local/bin/zig (version 0.16.0)
#>   [ok] C toolchain   C compiler clang

rzig_status() also reports, before anything is compiled, argument and return types the boundary rejects, more than 32 arguments, misuse of rzig.Mut([]f64), a missing registration block or panic handler in main.zig, R functions of the same name elsewhere in R/, framework sources from another rzig version, non-executable configure scripts and a missing C toolchain. A failed build names its cause:

rzig::build_zig(pkg, preflight = FALSE)
#> Build of package rzhello: failed at the compile step
#>   src/rzig/framework/convert.zig:138:9 (function total)
#>     rzig: function `total`, parameter 1 has unsupported type '[]const f32'.
#>     nearest supported alternative: []const f64 for an R numeric vector
#> The complete installation log (61 lines) is in $log.

5. Build and call. build_zig() runs the checks of rzig_status(), compiles and installs the package from a temporary copy, and reports the first compiler, linker or load error with its file and line when the build fails. The package also installs like any source package, with install.packages(pkg, repos = NULL, type = "source") or R CMD INSTALL.

build <- rzig::build_zig(pkg)
build
#> Build of package rzhello: succeeded in 8.1 seconds
#> Zig compiler: /usr/local/bin/zig (version 0.16.0)
#> Installed into a library in the session temporary directory
library(rzhello, lib.loc = build$library)

add_vectors(c(1, 2, 3), c(10, 20, 30))
#> [1] 11 22 33

add_vectors(c(1, 2), c(1, 2, 3))
#> Error: lengths differ: 2 vs 3

# The session remains usable after the native error.
add_vectors(c(4, 5), c(6, 7))
#> [1] 10 12

The same workflow applies to an existing package: run use_rzig() once, edit src/rzig/src/main.zig, and run document() whenever exported Zig signatures or comments change. The scaffolded cleanup and cleanup.win scripts remove generated Makevars and Zig build caches after package installation and checks. use_rzig() stops when src/ already holds C, C++ or Fortran sources (see the next section for such packages) or a hand-written src/Makevars, whose settings belong in src/Makevars.in and src/Makevars.win.in.

Packages with C, C++ or Fortran sources

use_rzig(path, mixed = TRUE) (or use_rzig_mixed(path) in a package that already uses rzig) sets Config/rzig/mixed: true. R then compiles every C, C++ and Fortran source of src/ with its own compilers and links them with the Zig library, and src/entry.c leaves R_init_<pkg> to the package. The package’s R_init_<pkg> registers its routines with rzig_register(), which adds the Zig routines to the .Call routines:

#include <R_ext/Rdynload.h>

void rzig_register(DllInfo *dll, const R_CMethodDef *c_methods,
                   const R_CallMethodDef *call_methods,
                   const R_FortranMethodDef *fortran_methods,
                   const R_ExternalMethodDef *external_methods);

static const R_CallMethodDef call_methods[] = {
    {"legacy_add", (DL_FUNC) &legacy_add, 2},
    {NULL, NULL, 0}
};

void R_init_mypkg(DllInfo *dll) {
    rzig_register(dll, NULL, call_methods, NULL, NULL);
}

The R code keeps its own useDynLib() directive for the C routines and may name them by symbol or by string. rzig_status() and build_zig() report a mixed package whose sources do not call rzig_register().

C libraries compiled by Zig

A package can ship the sources of a C library, for example under src/rzig/vendor/answer, and list it in src/rzig/c_libraries.zon. Zig compiles the sources into the package and translates the header into a Zig module; nothing is downloaded.

.{
    .{
        .name = "answer",
        .header = "vendor/answer/answer.h",
        .sources = .{"vendor/answer/answer.c"},
        .include = .{"vendor/answer"},
        .flags = .{"-std=c99"},
    },
}

The Zig sources then call the library through const answer = @import("answer");, also in the tests of test_zig(). Paths are relative to src/rzig; rzig_status() reports listed files that do not exist, and update_rzig() never replaces the file. The license and copyright of the vendored code belong in the package’s DESCRIPTION and inst/COPYRIGHTS.

Zig modules shared between packages

A package shares Zig code as a module: use_rzig_module(path, "kernels") creates inst/zig/kernels/root.zig, which R installs with the package. Another package uses it with use_rzig_import(path, "kernelpkg", "kernels"), which adds kernelpkg/kernels to Config/rzig/imports and kernelpkg to LinkingTo, so that R installs kernelpkg first. Its Zig code then imports the module:

const kernels = @import("kernels");

/// Twice the sum of the values.
/// @export
pub fn total(x: []const f64) f64 {
    return 2 * kernels.sum(x);
}

configure finds the module in the installed package, and the module is compiled into the importing package, so nothing is linked between packages at run time. A module can import rzig and the other imported modules; test_zig() passes the imports to the Zig tests as well.

C-callable functions between packages

Compiled code of other packages, in C or in Zig, can call functions that a package registers with R_RegisterCCallable(). The root Zig file lists them, each with callconv(.c), and may declare an interface version:

fn scaledSum(x: [*]const f64, n: usize, factor: f64) callconv(.c) f64 {
    var total: f64 = 0;
    for (x[0..n]) |value| total += value;
    return factor * total;
}

pub const rzig_callables = .{ .scaled_sum = scaledSum };
pub const rzig_interface_version: u32 = 2;

Another rzig package fetches one with rzig.callable(), which loads the namespace of the providing package and checks the interface version, because R checks neither the signature nor a version:

const ScaledSum = fn ([*]const f64, usize, f64) callconv(.c) f64;
const scaled_sum = try rzig.callable(ctx, ScaledSum, "provpkg", "scaled_sum", .{ .interface = 2 });

C code calls R_GetCCallable("provpkg", "scaled_sum") after loading the namespace; the providing package can declare the C signatures in inst/include. The calling package lists the providing one in Imports.

Compiling Zig from the R prompt

zig_function() compiles Zig code into a small package in the session’s temporary directory and defines its functions, like Rcpp::cppFunction():

twice <- rzig::zig_function("pub fn twice(x: f64) f64 { return 2 * x; }")
twice(21)
#> [1] 42
rzig::zig_eval("@sqrt(2.0)", type = "f64")
#> [1] 1.414214

zig_source(file) does the same for a file. Every top-level pub fn is exported unless the code marks functions with /// @export. Builds are cached for the session, and a compiler error is reported with the line of the code. In R Markdown and Quarto documents, a zig chunk compiles its code with zig_function() and later R chunks can call the functions.

Printing and progress

ctx.print() and ctx.eprint() format text with Zig’s std.fmt and write it to R’s output and message streams (Rprintf, REprintf), so it reaches the console, RStudio and sink(). ctx.progress(total, show) draws a progress bar on the message stream and checks for a user interrupt at each redraw:

/// @default verbose interactive()
/// @export
pub fn simulate(ctx: *rzig.Ctx, n: usize, verbose: bool) rzig.Error!f64 {
    var progress = ctx.progress(n, verbose);
    var total: f64 = 0;
    for (0..n) |i| {
        total += @sqrt(@as(f64, @floatFromInt(i)));
        try progress.add(1);
    }
    try progress.finish();
    return total;
}

All three need the call context, so they run on the R thread; a progress bar in the state of rzig.parallelFor workers is a compile error.

Debugging builds

Packages build in Zig’s ReleaseSafe mode: optimized, with the bounds, overflow and unreachable checks that the boundary turns into R errors. build_zig(path, optimize = "Debug"), or RZIG_OPTIMIZE=Debug in the environment of R CMD INSTALL, builds without optimization and with the same checks and complete stack traces. ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall are rejected, because they remove the checks; @setRuntimeSafety(false) removes them from a single function whose safety the package author has established.

Zig tests without R

test_zig(path) runs zig build test for a package: the test blocks of the files that src/rzig/src/tests.zig imports are compiled for the host and run without R, which suits numerical kernels written in plain Zig:

// src/rzig/src/tests.zig
test {
    _ = @import("kernels.zig");
}

Files that use the rzig module call into R and are tested from R (testthat). Packages scaffolded by an older rzig get the test step of build.zig from update_rzig(path).

Installing Zig

install_zig() downloads Zig 0.16.0 (or install_zig("0.17.0")) for the current platform into zig_home(), a folder in rzig’s user cache. The archive is checked against the size and SHA-256 that ziglang.org publishes, pinned in rzig, and comes from a community mirror of Zig or from ziglang.org. find_zig() and the configure scripts of rzig packages find compilers installed there; uninstall_zig() removes them.

Installing rzig packages on machines without Zig

The configure script of a package created with rzig downloads Zig itself when no supported compiler is found and the environment variable RZIG_DOWNLOAD_ZIG is true:

Sys.setenv(RZIG_DOWNLOAD_ZIG = "true")
install.packages("zigstats", repos = "https://example.r-universe.dev")

The download is the verified archive of install_zig() (Zig 0.16.0, or the release named by RZIG_ZIG_VERSION) and is kept in zig_home() for later installations. Without the variable, nothing is downloaded and the installation stops with instructions.

Creating a package

create_rzig_package("path/to/zigstats") creates a package named zigstats with the scaffold, the hello_zig() example, its help page and a testthat suite; build_zig("path/to/zigstats") installs it. Replace the placeholder title, description and author through fields:

rzig::create_rzig_package("zigstats", fields = list(
  Title = "Rank Statistics in 'Zig'",
  "Authors@R" = 'person("Ada", "Lovelace", email = "ada@example.org", role = c("aut", "cre"))'
))

Continuous integration

use_rzig_ci(path) writes .github/workflows/rzig-check.yaml, a GitHub Actions workflow that installs R and Zig 0.16.0 and 0.17.0 and runs R CMD check --as-cran on Linux, macOS and Windows, after the Zig tests when src/rzig/src/tests.zig exists. The zig and os arguments choose the matrix.

Export options

The marker line and @default lines shape the R wrapper:

/// Fit the model.
/// @param x The data.
/// @param tolerance The convergence tolerance.
/// @default tolerance 1e-8
/// @export name=fit_model invisible
pub fn fit_model_zig(x: []const f64, tolerance: f64) f64 { ... }

generates fit_model <- function(x, tolerance = 1e-8) invisible(...). The options are internal (see below), invisible and name=<R name>; any other option is an error of the scan.

Exports in several files

main.zig can collect exports from other files of src/rzig/src:

pub const stats = @import("stats.zig"); // exports in stats.zig are found
const helpers = @import("helpers.zig");

/// Three times a value.
/// @export
pub const triple = helpers.triple;       // re-exports helpers.triple as triple()

A function marked /// @export in a file that main.zig imports with pub const (directly or through another such file) is registered under its own name. A marker in a file imported with a plain const is an error, because the generated registration can reach only public declarations; a marked file that is not imported at all is ignored, and rzig_status() notes it. R names must be unique across all files.

Internal routines

A native routine that only the package’s own R code calls is marked /// @export internal. It is registered and gets an R wrapper, but the wrapper is not exported from the package and gets no help page:

/// Fit the penalized model for the R function fit_model().
/// @export internal
pub fn fit_model_zig(ctx: *rzig.Ctx, x: rzig.Matrix, y: []const f64) rzig.Error![]f64 {
    ...
}
fit_model <- function(x, y) {
  stopifnot(is.matrix(x), is.numeric(y))
  fit_model_zig(x, as.double(y))
}

Faster builds on a development machine

Every installation compiles in a fresh copy of the package, and Zig keeps its global cache inside that copy so that R CMD check and CRAN find nothing written outside the package. With Zig 0.17 the first step of each build then compiles Zig’s build runner again. On a development machine, a persistent cache avoids that:

Sys.setenv(RZIG_ZIG_CACHE = tools::R_user_dir("rzig", "cache"))

Leave RZIG_ZIG_CACHE unset for checks of a package before release.

Updating rzig in a package

After installing a new version of rzig, bring a package up to date with

rzig::update_rzig(pkg)

update_rzig() replaces the framework sources under src/rzig/framework, updates every build file that is still an unmodified rzig template, adds missing ones and regenerates the bindings. It never changes src/rzig/src or files rzig does not know, and it keeps build files the package author edited (for example a configure that downloads Zig, or a build.zig with an extra test step) and lists them, so their differences from the new templates can be reviewed. update_rzig(pkg, force = TRUE) replaces those as well. rzig_status() reports framework sources that do not match the installed rzig.

If roxygen2 generates NAMESPACE (its first line is # Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand), document() writes the native-symbol directive into R/rzig-wrappers.R as a @rawNamespace tag and adds the same lines roxygen2 writes to NAMESPACE. The package then works whichever of rzig::document(), roxygen2::roxygenise() or devtools::document() ran last, and roxygen2 writes the help pages of the exported Zig functions. Run rzig::document() after changing an exported Zig signature, so that the wrappers follow it. When devtools and rzig are both attached, one document() masks the other; call rzig::document() explicitly. If roxygenise() loaded the package in the current R session, restart R before calling newly installed native exports.

What document() generates

Every public Zig function with a /// @export line produces:

  • a compile-time Zig manifest entry;
  • an R wrapper with the visible Zig parameter names;
  • an explicitly resolved native symbol in NAMESPACE;
  • a roxygen block derived from the Zig doc comment; and
  • a help page man/<name>.Rd written from the same comment (the first paragraph gives the title and description; @param, @return, @examples, @details, @seealso, @references and @note fill their sections). In a package documented with roxygen2, roxygen2 writes the page from the roxygen block instead.

The first *rzig.Ctx parameter is supplied by RZig and omitted from the R function. The complete input surface is:

Zig parameter Accepted R value Conversion
f64 length-one double, integer, or logical checked scalar
i32 length-one double, integer, or logical checked whole number
bool length-one logical checked scalar
usize length-one double, integer, or logical checked whole number from 0 to 2147483647
i64 length-one bit64::integer64, double, or integer checked whole number; doubles up to 2^53 - 1 in absolute value
?f64, ?i32, ?bool, ?usize, ?i64 corresponding scalar, NA, or NULL missing values become null
[]const f64 double vector borrowed, read-only
[]const i32 integer vector borrowed, read-only
[]const i64 bit64::integer64 vector borrowed, read-only; NA is rzig.NA.integer64
[]const bool logical vector without NA copied into the call arena
[]const rzig.Logical logical vector borrowed, read-only; elements .TRUE, .FALSE, .NA
[]const u8 one non-NA character value copied as UTF-8
[]const []const u8 character vector without NA copied as UTF-8
[]const ?[]const u8 character vector copied as UTF-8; NA becomes null
?[]const u8 one character value, NA, or NULL copied as UTF-8; NA and NULL become null
rzig.Complex length-one complex, double, or integer checked scalar; NA errors
[]const rzig.Complex complex vector borrowed, read-only, layout of Rcomplex
rzig.Raw raw vector borrowed bytes in .data
rzig.Record(T) named list entries read into the fields of struct T by name; defaults fill missing entries
rzig.DataFrame(T) data frame columns read into the fields of struct T; .nrow rows
rzig.Factor factor .codes borrowed, .levels copied
rzig.CscMatrix Matrix::dgCMatrix slots i, p, x borrowed and checked; column(j)
?T T, or NULL NULL becomes null (scalars also map NA to null)
rzig.Matrix double matrix borrowed, read-only, column-major
rzig.IntMatrix integer matrix borrowed, read-only, column-major; NA is std.math.minInt(i32)
rzig.BoolMatrix logical matrix without NA copied into the call arena
rzig.Mut([]f64), rzig.Mut([]i32) double or integer vector duplicated before writable access
rzig.Mut(rzig.Matrix), rzig.Mut(rzig.IntMatrix) double or integer matrix duplicated with its attributes before writable access
rzig.Sexp any R object borrowed low-level handle
rzig.Function function borrowed; call() evaluates it from Zig

Supported return values are:

Zig return R result
void NULL
f64, i32, bool length-one double, integer, or logical
i64, []const i64 / []i64 bit64::integer64 value or vector
[]const f64 / []f64 double vector
[]const i32 / []i32 integer vector
[]const bool / []bool logical vector
[]const rzig.Logical / []rzig.Logical logical vector that can contain NA
[]const u8 length-one character vector
[]const []const u8 / [][]const u8 character vector
[]const ?[]const u8 / []?[]const u8 character vector; null becomes NA
rzig.Complex length-one complex vector
[]const rzig.Complex / []rzig.Complex complex vector
rzig.Raw raw vector
rzig.Record(T) / rzig.DataFrame(T) named list / data frame built from the fields of T
rzig.Factor factor
rzig.List named R list
rzig.Attributed(T) supported vector T with names, dimensions, dimnames, or classes
rzig.Sexp the supplied R object
rzig.Function the supplied function
?T supported T, or NULL when null

Any supported return may be wrapped in rzig.Error!T. usize and the matrix views are parameter-only. Unsupported signatures fail at compile time with the function and parameter position in the error.

Errors and warnings

rzig.raise() records a message and returns rzig.Error, so it can be returned directly or propagated with try. rzig.warn() queues a warning for delivery after Zig cleanup and returns void, so call it without try:

if (values.len == 0) rzig.warn("received an empty vector", .{});

Returning named lists

rzig.List collects supported return values in Zig-owned memory and converts them to one named R list only after the function returns:

/// Return values together with their length.
/// @export
pub fn summarize(ctx: *rzig.Ctx, values: []const f64) rzig.Error!rzig.List {
    if (values.len > std.math.maxInt(i32)) return rzig.raise("too many values", .{});
    var result = rzig.List.init(ctx);
    try result.put("values", values);
    try result.put("count", @as(i32, @intCast(values.len)));
    return result;
}

List entries may contain f64, i32, bool, double, integer, or logical slices, UTF-8 strings or string vectors, optional values, or rzig.Sexp. Names are copied into the call context, and no R object is allocated until boundary conversion begins.

Lists, data frames and factors

rzig.Record(T) reads a named list into the struct T, field by field; a field with a default value may be missing from the list, an optional field becomes null, and an unknown entry gives a warning. One record argument carries any number of values, beyond the 32 arguments of a function:

const Options = struct {
    tolerance: f64 = 1e-8,
    @"max.iter": i32 = 100,
    weights: ?[]const f64 = null,
};

/// @export
pub fn fit(x: []const f64, options: rzig.Record(Options)) f64 {
    _ = options.value.@"max.iter";
    return x[0] * options.value.tolerance;
}

rzig.DataFrame(T) reads the columns of a data frame (slices or rzig.Factor) and its number of rows; other columns are ignored, and every column must have one value per row. rzig.Factor holds the 1-based codes and the levels of a factor. All three are also return types: a record becomes a named list, a data frame gets compact row names, and a factor’s codes are checked against its levels.

Classes

A struct marked /// @class becomes an R class: init is the constructor, exported under the struct’s name, and every public function that takes the struct as its first parameter is a method, called with $:

/// A running mean.
/// @class
pub const RunningMean = struct {
    total: f64 = 0,
    count: usize = 0,

    /// Create an empty running mean.
    pub fn init() RunningMean {
        return .{};
    }

    /// Add values.
    pub fn add(self: *RunningMean, values: []const f64) void {
        for (values) |value| self.total += value;
        self.count += values.len;
    }

    /// The mean of the values added so far.
    pub fn mean(self: *const RunningMean) f64 {
        return self.total / @as(f64, @floatFromInt(self.count));
    }
};
m <- RunningMean()
m$add(c(1, 2, 3))
m$mean()
#> [1] 2

document() generates the constructor, a $ method, a print method that lists the methods, completion of method names, and a help page with a Methods section; the object is an rzig.External(RunningMean).

Values that live across calls

rzig.External(T) keeps a Zig value between calls in an R object (an external pointer with the classes c("T", "rzig_external")). A function returns rzig.External(T).create(ctx, value), and later calls receive the value through .ptr and may modify it; when R garbage-collects the object, T.deinit() runs (it must not call R) and the memory is released:

const Counter = struct {
    count: i32 = 0,
    pub fn deinit(self: *Counter) void {
        _ = self;
    }
};

/// @export
pub fn counter(ctx: *rzig.Ctx) rzig.Error!rzig.External(Counter) {
    return rzig.External(Counter).create(ctx, .{});
}

/// @export
pub fn increment(c: rzig.External(Counter)) i32 {
    c.ptr.count += 1;
    return c.ptr.count;
}

Memory that the value refers to must outlive the call: allocate it with std.heap.c_allocator and free it in deinit, not with the call context. An object of another type or package is rejected by its tag. A value saved with saveRDS() or in a workspace is lost, and using it is an error that asks to create it again.

Reading R objects

An rzig.Sexp parameter borrows any R object. Its read-only methods report kind() (.double, .list, .s4, …), length(), isNull(), isObject(), isS4() and inherits(class), read attribute(name) (S4 slots are attributes), names(ctx) and classes(ctx), walk a list with element(index) and field(name), and convert a value with get(T, ctx) by the rules of a parameter of type T:

/// @export
pub fn total(ctx: *rzig.Ctx, value: rzig.Sexp) rzig.Error!f64 {
    const entry = (try value.field("x")) orelse return rzig.raise("no entry x", .{});
    var sum: f64 = 0;
    for (try entry.get([]const f64, ctx)) |x| sum += x;
    return sum;
}

Mutable inputs

Mutation is opt-in with rzig.Mut([]f64), rzig.Mut([]i32), rzig.Mut(rzig.Matrix) or rzig.Mut(rzig.IntMatrix). RZig duplicates and protects the R vector or matrix before Zig receives writable storage, then returns that duplicate, which keeps the attributes of the input (dim, dimnames, class):

/// Scale a copy of a numeric vector.
/// @export
pub fn scale(values: rzig.Mut([]f64), factor: f64) void {
    for (values.data) |*value| value.* *= factor;
}

The caller’s vector and any aliases remain unchanged. A function using Mut accepts one mutable vector and returns void or rzig.Error!void; its generated R wrapper returns the mutated duplicate automatically.

Attributes and matrices

rzig.Matrix borrows an R double matrix in column-major order and provides its validated shape through nrow and ncol; rzig.IntMatrix borrows an integer matrix, and rzig.BoolMatrix copies a logical matrix without NA. at(row, column) reads one element and column(j) returns one column as a slice (zero-based indices). A matrix of another storage mode is rejected with the storage.mode() call that converts it in R. rzig.Mut(rzig.Matrix) exposes set(row, column, value) as well:

/// Center each column of a numeric matrix.
/// @export
pub fn center_columns(values: rzig.Mut(rzig.Matrix)) void {
    for (0..values.data.ncol) |j| {
        const column = values.data.column(j);
        var mean: f64 = 0;
        for (column) |value| mean += value;
        mean /= @floatFromInt(column.len);
        for (column) |*value| value.* -= mean;
    }
}

Use rzig.Attributed([]const f64) to return a numeric vector with metadata:

pub fn labeled(
    ctx: *rzig.Ctx,
    values: []const f64,
    labels: []const []const u8,
) rzig.Error!rzig.Attributed([]const f64) {
    var result = rzig.Attributed([]const f64).init(ctx, values);
    try result.setNames(labels);
    try result.setClass("labeled_values");
    return result;
}

setNames, setDim, setClass, and setClasses copy their metadata into the call context; setMatrix(nrow, ncol) sets a two-dimensional dim and setDimnames(row_names, column_names) names the rows and columns (null leaves a dimension unnamed). Lengths and dimension products are checked before R allocation.

Long-running loops

Call try rzig.checkInterrupt() about every 100,000 iterations of a long loop. It probes through an R trampoline that catches the runtime’s non-local interrupt exit, allowing Zig cleanup to finish before the boundary returns an R error.

Distributions

rzig.Rmath.density, rzig.Rmath.cdf and rzig.Rmath.quantile evaluate the distributions of R (.normal, .uniform, .gamma, .beta, .binomial, .poisson, .exponential, .t, .chisq, .f, .lognormal, .weibull, .logistic, .cauchy, .geometric, .hypergeometric, .negative_binomial), with R’s parameter names and defaults, and rng.draw(distribution, params) draws from R’s generator, so the draws follow set.seed():

const p = try rzig.Rmath.cdf(.gamma, x, .{ .shape = 2 }, .{ .lower_tail = false });
const d = try rzig.Rmath.density(.normal, x, .{ .mean = 1 }, .{ .log = true });
const rng = try ctx.rng();
const draw = rng.draw(.poisson, .{ .lambda = 3 });

Reductions, random streams and interrupts in parallel loops

rzig.parallelReduce(ctx, T, count, &state, identity, map, combine) reduces map(state, i) with combine in chunks fixed by count, so a parallel floating-point sum is the same for every number of threads. ctx.rngStreams() gives workers random streams seeded from R’s stream: streams.stream(i) is the same for the same seed and index, so parallel draws follow set.seed(). A user interrupt stops the workers after their current index, and a panic on a worker (for example a failed bounds check) becomes an R error instead of ending the session.

Linear algebra

rzig.Blas (gemm, gemv, syrk, trsm) and rzig.Lapack (potrf, potrs, getrf, getrs, gesv, geqrf, ormqr, gels, syevr, gesdd) call the BLAS and LAPACK that R uses, on column-major matrices: rzig.Matrix operands and rzig.MutableMatrix results, for example from ctx.matrix(nrow, ncol) or rzig.Mut(rzig.Matrix). Every routine checks the shapes before the call and turns LAPACK’s info into an R error, such as “the matrix is not positive definite”. A package that uses them runs use_rzig_lapack(path) once, so that it links $(LAPACK_LIBS) $(BLAS_LIBS) $(FLIBS):

/// @export
pub fn crossprod(ctx: *rzig.Ctx, x: rzig.Matrix) rzig.Error!rzig.Attributed([]f64) {
    const out = try ctx.matrix(x.ncol, x.ncol);
    try rzig.Blas.gemm(ctx, .yes, .no, 1, x, x, 0, out);
    var result = rzig.Attributed([]f64).init(ctx, out.data);
    try result.setMatrix(out.nrow, out.ncol);
    return result;
}

Calling R functions from Zig

An rzig.Function parameter receives an R function, and f.call(ctx, T, args) calls it on the thread that entered R. args is a tuple of positional arguments or a struct of named ones, with values of any type an exported function can return; the result is converted to T like an argument (void ignores it).

pub fn apply_twice(ctx: *rzig.Ctx, f: rzig.Function, x: []const f64) rzig.Error![]const f64 {
    const once = try f.call(ctx, []const f64, .{x});
    return f.call(ctx, []const f64, .{ .x = once });
}

An R error, an interrupt, or a condition handler or restart outside the call that takes control returns rzig.Error. Return it, and R continues the error with its class and call once the Zig frames have run their defer blocks, so tryCatch(), withCallingHandlers() and traceback() behave as they would without Zig in between. The calls appear as f(...), with the name of the R argument. A borrowed result stays allocated until the exported function returns, and R’s random-number state passes to R and back when ctx.rng() is in use. Objectives and integrands of rzig.Optimize and rzig.Integrate may call R functions.

Optimization and integration

rzig.Optimize.minimize(ctx, method, &problem, x, options) runs the optimizers of optim() (.bfgs, .nelder_mead, .conjugate_gradient, .lbfgsb with bounds) on a Zig objective: problem has value(x) and, optionally, gradient(x, g); without one, central differences use the step of optim(). rzig.Integrate.integrate(ctx, &f, lower, upper, .{}) integrates f.value(x) as integrate() does, with infinite limits allowed. Errors of the callbacks are reported when the routine finishes.

const Problem = struct {
    data: []const f64,
    pub fn value(self: *const Problem, x: []const f64) f64 {
        var total: f64 = 0;
        for (self.data) |y| total += (y - x[0]) * (y - x[0]);
        return total;
    }
};

const x = try ctx.dupe(f64, &.{0.0});
const result = try rzig.Optimize.minimize(ctx, .bfgs, &Problem{ .data = data }, x, .{});

Pure Zig parallel loops

rzig.parallelFor distributes an indexed computation across Zig worker threads. Its state is checked at compile time: Ctx, Sexp, matrices, list builders, mutable inputs, attributed results, opaque pointers, and function pointers cannot cross into a worker.

const Work = struct {
    input: []const f64,
    output: []f64,

    fn square(work: *@This(), index: usize) void {
        work.output[index] = work.input[index] * work.input[index];
    }
};

pub fn squares(ctx: *rzig.Ctx, input: []const f64) rzig.Error![]f64 {
    const output = try ctx.alloc(f64, input.len);
    var work = Work{ .input = input, .output = output };
    try rzig.parallelFor(ctx, input.len, &work, Work.square);
    return output;
}

The callback has the exact signature fn(*State, usize) void and always runs off the R thread. It must be panic-free and must not import or call R or RZig APIs. If a worker can fail, record that in atomic plain-data state, wait for parallelFor to join every worker, and call rzig.raise on the calling thread.

parallelFor starts one worker thread per core, at most 32 and at most one per index. The environment variable RZIG_NUM_THREADS lowers that number (for example Sys.setenv(RZIG_NUM_THREADS = 2) in R), OMP_THREAD_LIMIT is respected as well, and while R CMD check limits the cores (_R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_, set for CRAN submissions) at most two threads run, as the CRAN policy requires. rzig.parallelThreadCount(count) returns the number of threads a call would use, for example to size per-thread buffers.

Safety model

RZig keeps R’s non-local error mechanism at the outer native boundary. Internal Zig code returns explicit errors, all Zig-owned cleanup finishes before an R error is raised, and cleanup is protected if an R API call jumps out. A jump of R out of R code that Zig calls (rzig.Function) stops before the Zig frames and resumes after them. Inputs are borrowed read-only, return slices are copied into R-owned memory, and generated packages build in ReleaseSafe mode so bounds and overflow checks stay enabled.

R’s API remains single-threaded. Zig code may parallelize pure computation, but must not call R from worker threads.

Development checks

The package tests run with R CMD check and need no Zig. The repository test suite runs with Zig 0.16.0 and 0.17.0:

zig build test
zig build --release=safe
zig build lint
R CMD build tests/fixtures/rzigtest

Continuous integration builds and checks the fixture package on Linux, macOS, and Windows, and runs GC-stress and memory-analysis profiles where available.

Stability

From version 1.0.0, rzig follows semantic versioning for its public interface: the exported R functions, the declarations of the Zig module rzig except rzig.internal, the markers and options of the Zig source (/// @export, /// @class, @default), the fields of DESCRIPTION that it reads (Config/rzig/...), and the files it writes into a package. A change that breaks code using them comes with a new major version; additions come with minor versions. rzig.internal, the generated manifest and the framework files under src/rzig/framework are rzig’s own and change with any version; update_rzig() replaces them.

Zig changes between release series, so rzig supports the two most recent series it has been tested with (0.16 and 0.17 for rzig 1.0.0). Support for a new series comes with a minor version; a series is dropped in a minor version that NEWS announces one version ahead.
